title: Nvidia in talks to guarantee $250 billion of OpenAI's Ohio data-center financing
subtitle: The reported backstop would cover OpenAI's lease of a $500-billion, 10-gigawatt SoftBank-led campus near Piketon, Ohio — the largest financial guarantee ever discussed between two private companies.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg reported on July 26 that Nvidia is in early talks to guarantee roughly $250 billion of financing for OpenAI's lease of a planned 10-gigawatt data-center campus in southern Ohio, near Piketon. The site is being developed by SB Energy, a SoftBank energy subsidiary, at a total build cost estimated above $500 billion. The first 800-megawatt phase is targeted for 2028. A financial guarantee is a contractual promise by one company to cover another's payment obligations if the counterparty defaults — routine at small scale in commercial lending, but at $250 billion this would be the largest ever recorded between two private companies. Talks are described as ongoing and could still change or fall apart.

The structure is unusual on purpose. OpenAI has never carried an investment-grade credit rating, so leasing a hyperscale campus at this size would normally require either a hyperscaler cosigner or a sovereign-grade counterparty. Nvidia stepping in as guarantor lets OpenAI sign the lease at rates closer to an investment-grade tenant while Nvidia locks in a decade-plus baseline of chip demand from the site. SoftBank gets a de-risked developer role. The trade is that Nvidia now sits on both sides of a large chunk of the AI capex cycle — selling the chips and underwriting the credit that pays for them — which is exactly the concentration of risk investor Michael Burry flagged when he wrote 'around and around we go' about the arrangement.

This is the second week in a row that a nine- or ten-figure infrastructure announcement has reshaped the buildout map. Nvidia and SK Group signed a $500-billion-plus AI factories and memory partnership on July 24-25, including a 2-gigawatt Vera Rubin data center in South Korea and an HBM4 memory-supply lock-in with SK Hynix. Alphabet raised 2026 capex guidance to $195-205 billion on its Q2 call. Meta is expected to report on July 29 with its own capex range in play. The pattern is that the four US frontier labs, the two US hyperscalers building for them, and their chip supplier are all pre-committing capacity through 2030 in deals that individually match a mid-size national budget.

For learners: when the same chip supplier both sells the chips and guarantees the debt that buys them, ask what happens to the deal if demand for those chips softens. The AI infrastructure buildout is being financed on the assumption that model capability and enterprise demand keep compounding at their current pace. That may well hold — but the way to read announcements like this one is not 'AI is winning' but 'AI's largest players are betting that AI will keep winning at a specific rate.' If you are building a career or a product around AI, that is useful context: the incumbents are locking in enough compute for a much larger economy of AI usage than exists today, and someone has to actually build that usage.
